A short visitor's guide to how the town gets its drinking water.

The supply starts high in the hills, where a dam holds back a large lake of rain and snowmelt.
Two buried pipes lead from that dam down to the pumps, so water never has to wait on one line.
Either of those pipes can move roughly four megalitres in a single day.
When the lake brims after the spring thaw, it can keep the town going for about three months.
Metal grilles at the mouths of the pipes stop leaves, small fish and drifting rubbish.
Each autumn one pipe is shut and scrubbed while its twin carries the whole load.
Staff check how full the lake is at dawn and chalk the figure up inside the office.

Inside the plant, incoming water is stirred with a chemical that makes tiny specks clump.
Those clumps sink, and the clearer water above them moves on toward the filter beds.
Half a dozen beds of sand catch nearly all the grit that is still floating along.
On alternate days the beds are flushed backwards with clean water to shift the caught silt.
Only once the water has been filtered does it receive its dose of disinfectant.
That disinfectant keeps the supply wholesome as it travels through the pipes under the roads.
Staff on duty sample the disinfectant strength at intervals of four hours, round the clock.
Each result goes into a logbook that lives on a table in the plant's main room.
Before a shift ends, a colleague countersigns that book and then the next team takes over.

From the plant, pumps push the clean water up a slope to a roofed reservoir near the old square.
That roofed reservoir can meet a full day's demand from every household in town.
No pumps are needed after that point, because the slope lets water run down to each road.
Under the old square, pipes laid in iron long ago are being swapped for modern plastic ones.
Crews look for hidden leaks after dark, since that is when the fewest taps are running.
If a pipe bursts, an on-call team can arrive anywhere in town inside sixty minutes.

Eleven staff keep the works running, split between three rotating shifts and an office day.
A newcomer spends a month and a half shadowing an experienced colleague first.
Only after that training period may a newcomer run the plant without a partner.
Each month a quality summary goes to the councillors, and a copy hangs in the public library.
Hours on every pump are noted each week, so motors get attention before they fail.
A replacement motor waits in a storeroom right next to the repair shop entrance.

Some practical questions come up often from visitors on the guided walk.
People ask why there are two pipes from the dam, and the answer is simply resilience.
If one line needs work, the other one keeps the plant supplied without a pause.
Visitors are often surprised that sand, of all things, does most of the cleaning.
The grit caught by the beds would otherwise cloud every glass poured in town.
Washing the sand in reverse is quick, and the dirty rinse water is settled before release.
The disinfectant is added late in the process so that it is not wasted on muddy water.
Results from the four-hourly checks are kept for years in case anyone questions them.
A signed handover means nobody can quietly skip a reading during a long night.

The covered reservoir above the square also acts as a buffer during busy mornings.
When everyone showers at once, it smooths out the demand on the pumps below.
Replacing the iron pipes is slow work, done a few streets at a time each summer.
Night surveys use listening rods that pick up the hiss of water escaping underground.
The on-call team carries spare pipe sections in a van parked beside the works.
The office day shift handles billing, visitor bookings and the monthly paperwork.
Trainees keep a notebook of every task they have watched before they try it alone.
The weekly pump records help the fitters plan repairs for the quiet winter months.
Keeping a spare motor on site means a breakdown costs hours rather than weeks.
Guides end the walk at the filter beds, where visitors can see the sand for themselves.
